references.text: Moses conveys the same call for voluntary gifts to the sanctuary, where everyone with a willing heart is to bring an offering to the Lord.
The people respond to the call with willing hearts and bring gifts for the work of the tabernacle.
Describes how the people continued to bring voluntary gifts every morning for the sanctuary work.
The Lord speaks about the gifts and the terumah (heave offering) that are given to the priests.
Each man shall give according to his ability, in proportion to the blessing the Lord your God has given you—the principle of voluntary and proportional giving.
David and the people gave willingly with joy to the house of the Lord, with a whole heart.
David acknowledges that everything comes from God, and that voluntary gifts are actually returning what belongs to the Lord.
Under King Joash, voluntary gifts were collected from the people to restore the house of the Lord.
Paul teaches that a gift is welcome according to what one has, not according to what one does not have—the principle of voluntary and cheerful giving.
Each should give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
Both verses link the voluntary offering with a willing will/heart on the part of the giver.
Clear contrast: Exodus presents the ideal voluntary offering, while Amos criticizes the false misuse of the same concept.
Theological depth: The requirement for a willing heart (Exodus) is met by God's promise to give a new heart (Ezekiel).
The same event told as a command (chapter 25) and as its fulfillment (chapter 35).
